title: how-to guide for aspiring authors|outlining a non-fiction book before writing the first draft
text:
Before you write the first chapter of your non-fiction book, build a roadmap. Many first-time authors fear that outlining will stifle creativity, but in non-fiction, structure is what sets your ideas free. Without it, you risk writing in circles, repeating yourself, or leaving gaps that confuse the reader. A solid outline transforms a vague concept into a book that earns its place on a shelf.

Start by defining the transformation you want for your reader. Non-fiction is never just about information; it is about change. Ask what your reader believes or does before opening the book, and what they should believe or do after closing it. Write this transformation in one sentence. This becomes your North Star. Every chapter and example must serve this purpose. If an idea does not move the reader closer to that outcome, it does not belong.

Next, brainstorm without judgment. Set a timer for twenty minutes and list every concept, story, statistic, and argument related to your topic. Do not worry about order. When time is up, look for natural clusters. You will likely find three to seven major themes that want to become chapters. Move sticky notes or index cards until the logic feels inevitable. You are looking for the architecture already hiding inside your material.

Once your themes emerge, choose a structure that fits your content. Chronological order works for memoir and history. Step-by-step frameworks suit how-to books. Problem-solution structures fit books that diagnose a pain point and offer relief. If your chapters can stand alone, a modular structure may serve you best. There is no universal right choice, only the one that makes your argument clearest.

Then build your chapter outlines. For each chapter, write a short paragraph explaining what it covers and why it matters at that point in the book. List the key points in order. Under each point, note the evidence you will use, whether research, case studies, or expert quotes. Be specific enough that future-you will not face a blank page, but leave room for discovery while drafting. A good outline balances direction with flexibility.

Pay close attention to transitions. Non-fiction fails when readers bounce between disconnected essays. Ask how each chapter hands off to the next. Does Chapter Two answer a question raised in Chapter One? Note these bridges in your outline so you build them when you draft.

Check your outline for balance. Spread your strongest material across the book rather than front-loading it. Make sure no chapter is so packed it would require fifty pages while another barely fills ten. If one section keeps growing, consider whether it wants to become two chapters.

Your outline is a tool, not a prison. You may discover a better argument while drafting, and that is fine. The outline gives you permission to explore because you always know where home is. If you wander too far, you can find your way back.

When the outline feels solid, let it rest for a few days. Return with fresh eyes and read it straight through as if you were browsing the table of contents and summaries. If the journey feels coherent and compelling, you are ready to write. If something feels slow or redundant, fix it now. It is far easier to rearrange an outline than to restructure a finished manuscript.

Trust the process. The hours you spend outlining will save you weeks of rewriting, and they will ensure that when you finally sit down to draft, you know exactly what you need to say.

title: how-to guide for aspiring authors|outlining a non-fiction book before writing the first draft
text:
The Map Before the Territory: How to Outline a Nonfiction Book

Ask a room full of first-time authors how they plan to write their book and most will say some version of the same thing: sit down, open a blank document, and begin. Ask a room full of published authors and you will hear something different. Nearly all of them outline, and the ones who claim they don't usually turn out to be carrying the outline in their heads. For nonfiction especially, where the book's value lies in the clarity of its argument, writing without a plan is how you end up with 80,000 words of eloquent wandering.

So before you draft a single chapter, do the unglamorous work. Here is a method that has served me well across several books.

Start with one sentence. Not a paragraph, not a page. One sentence that states what your book argues or promises. "Sleep is the most underrated performance tool of the modern era." "Personal finance is a behavior problem, not a math problem." If you cannot compress your book into a sentence, you do not yet have a book; you have a topic. Tape that sentence above your desk. Every chapter you outline later must serve it.

Next, define your reader and the transformation. Who picks up this book, and who are they when they finish it? Nonfiction sells a change: from confused to competent, from anxious to equipped. Write a short paragraph describing that reader's starting point and destination. This will discipline every choice that follows, because a chapter that does not move the reader toward the destination does not belong in the book.

Then empty your head. Set aside a few days for a brain dump: every fact, study, anecdote, case study, interview fragment, and half-formed idea you might want to use. Do not organize yet. Index cards are ideal for this, one idea per card, but a long document works too. Most aspiring authors are surprised by how much material they already have, and alarmed by the gaps. Both discoveries are useful.

Now choose a structure. Nonfiction books tend to follow one of a handful of shapes: chronological, thematic, problem and solution, or a sequence of big questions. Look at your pile of material and ask which shape it naturally wants. A memoir-driven business book wants chronology; a practical guide wants problem and solution. Forcing material into the wrong shape is the quiet reason many manuscripts stall at chapter four.

With a structure chosen, build the chapter outline. Aim for ten to fourteen chapters unless you have reason otherwise. For each chapter, write a working title, one line stating its job in the argument, and three to five beats covering what it will actually contain, including which stories and evidence from your brain dump live there. Assign a rough word count to each. When you finish, you should be able to read the outline start to finish in two minutes and hear the book's logic unfold.

Test it before you trust it. Read the chapter summaries aloud. Look for repeated points, missing steps, and chapters carrying too much weight. Then hand the outline to one honest reader, ideally someone in your target audience, and ask a single question: where did I lose you?

Finally, hold the outline loosely. It is a map, not a contract. Every working author I know has watched a chapter split in two or a brilliant idea arrive mid-draft and demand a detour. Let it. The outline's real job is not to constrain the writing but to free it, because once you know where the book is going, you can stop worrying about the destination and give your full attention to the sentence in front of you. That, in the end, is what readers feel on the page.

title: self-publishing handbook|choosing a book title and cover that sell
text:
Titles and Covers: Earn the Click Before You Ask for the Love

My first crime novel was called *The Winter Archive*. I adored that title, which should have been my first warning. At a library event in Norwich, three readers asked if it was about Arctic exploration. It was about a murdered estate agent in Croydon. The book sold 211 copies in its first year, most of them, I suspect, to people who had met me.

When I relaunched it as *No Forwarding Address*, with a cover showing an empty hallway and one crooked door chain, monthly sales went from 19 to 104 over the next quarter. Same book. Well, nearly: I also fixed the flabby first chapter. Packaging is not magic. It simply stops good work being ignored for the wrong reasons.

A title has two jobs: survive being said aloud and signal the shelf. If someone hears it on a podcast, can they spell it into a search box? If a bookseller reads it once, can they repeat it? “Beautiful” is optional. Search the title before you fall in love. If it already belongs to a bestselling novel, a diet supplement and a Belgian metal band, keep walking.

For nonfiction, clarity usually beats charm. Dana Okafor, a career coach I worked with, wanted to call her book *The Unfolding*. We talked her into *Interview After 40*, with the subtitle *A Practical Guide to Getting Hired Without Pretending You’re 25*. She still thinks the subtitle is too long. She also received 73 pre-orders in the week the new cover went up, against 12 for the old version.

Now the cover. It is not a summary of chapter fourteen. It is a filing instruction for a stranger moving at speed. Screenshot the top twenty books in your category and study them without flinching. If every successful thriller is black, red and shouty, your tasteful watercolour cottage had better be hiding a body—and look like it.

Hire a designer who already makes covers in your genre. Send five comparison titles and one useful sentence: “Domestic suspense; danger inside an ordinary home; readers of Lisa Jewell.” Do not send a map of the village, a description of your heroine’s cheekbones and a request for “something like *Gone Girl*, but different.” That is not a brief. It is a nervous condition.

For a competent genre designer, budget roughly £250–£600; custom illustration costs more. I once paid £850 for a gorgeous literary cover that looked, at thumbnail size, like a grey sock. Cheap can be expensive. So can expensive.

Finally, shrink the cover to 120 pixels wide. Show it to five actual genre readers for three seconds. Ask, “What kind of book is this, and what can you read?” Not “Do you like it?” Your friends like you; their opinions are compromised.

A title earns the pause. A cover confirms the promise. Let the blurb do the seducing; packaging has a shift to work.

title: popular science book|what black holes reveal about space and time
text:
Chapter 6: The Hole in the Map

The first time I saw the Event Horizon Telescope’s image of M87*, I had to remind myself what I was looking at. The glowing ring was hot gas, not the black hole. The dark center was a shadow shaped by gravity bending light near the event horizon—the boundary beyond which no signal can return. It looked less like an object than like an absence. Yet that absence could weigh billions of Suns.

A black hole is often introduced as a place where gravity becomes overwhelmingly strong. That is true, but it misses the deeper surprise. In general relativity, gravity is not simply a force pulling objects across a fixed stage. Matter and energy change the geometry of spacetime, and moving objects follow the straightest paths available through that geometry. Usually, the distortion is modest enough that I can ignore it. A black hole is what happens when I cannot: space and time stop being the background and become the main actors.

Imagine that I watch a friend fall toward one, carrying a clock and flashing a light once every second. My friend experiences each tick normally. But the signals sent back to me arrive farther and farther apart, their light shifted toward longer, redder wavelengths. As my friend approaches the horizon, the delays grow without limit. The traveler appears to slow, redden, and fade. I never receive a flash announcing, “I have crossed.”

It is tempting to call this merely an optical illusion. My friend’s account, however, is equally valid. For a sufficiently large black hole, the crossing can occur after a finite interval on the traveler’s clock, with nothing dramatic marking the moment. There is no solid surface and no necessary local jolt. The horizon is a causal boundary: once across it, my friend cannot send news back to me, however powerful the transmitter.

The two accounts do not agree about what happens when, because there is no universal “when” standing above them. Each clock measures time along its own path through spacetime. Black holes make this impossible to dismiss as a technicality. They turn the relativity of time into a difference between receiving a final message and crossing a frontier.

Inside that frontier, the geometry becomes stranger still. Every path toward the future leads farther inward. In the simplest black hole, the central singularity is therefore not best imagined as a distant place I might steer around. It lies ahead more like an unavoidable event in the future. General relativity predicts infinite curvature there, but most physicists read that infinity as a warning: the theory has reached the edge of its authority. A quantum theory of gravity must take over.

These are not only theorists’ fantasies. Merging black holes have been detected through gravitational waves—ripples in spacetime itself. After collision, the new black hole “rings down,” settling into a quieter state much as a struck bell settles after ringing. The measured vibrations match general relativity’s predictions with remarkable precision.

Then quantum theory adds another twist. Stephen Hawking’s calculation, still awaiting direct astronomical confirmation, implies that black holes are not perfectly black. Quantum effects near the horizon should make them radiate and, over immense spans of time, evaporate. But Hawking’s radiation appears almost featureless, while quantum theory suggests that information cannot simply be erased. What happens to the detailed record of everything that fell in? The question remains open, and its answer may change my understanding of spacetime itself.

I used to think of space as where things happen and time as what clocks measure while they happen. Black holes make both definitions feel too small. Geometry can bend, flow, and ring; a clock measures its own history, not the universe’s. Black holes are not just exotic objects scattered across the cosmic map. They are places where the map’s assumptions become visible—and where, at the deepest level, the map begins to fail.

title: healthy eating guide|why whole grains and legumes should replace processed snacks
text:
In the rhythm of modern life, the snack drawer has become something of a sanctuary. Between meetings, school runs, and the general hum of obligation, it is often the processed snack that wins our affection. Yet the fleeting comfort of a bag of chips or a sugary granola bar comes at a cost that extends far beyond the empty wrapper. If we are serious about sustaining our energy, protecting our health, and quieting the relentless cycle of craving, we must reconsider what deserves space between our main meals. Whole grains and legumes, humble and ancient as they are, offer a genuinely satisfying alternative to the processed snacks that now dominate our diets.

The trouble with processed snacks is not merely one of excess calories, though that alone would be reason enough to pause. More concerning is how these foods are engineered to bypass our body’s natural signals. Stripped of fiber and loaded with refined carbohydrates, added sugars, and sodium, they rush into the bloodstream, spike glucose levels, and leave us reaching for the next fix just as quickly as the first. They are, in essence, designed for consumption rather than nourishment. Over time, this pattern strains insulin sensitivity, encourages visceral fat accumulation, and keeps us locked in a state of perpetual hunger disguised as convenience.

Whole grains present a starkly different proposition. Oats, quinoa, brown rice, and whole wheat still carry the bran and germ that refining removes, meaning they arrive intact with fiber, B vitamins, magnesium, and antioxidants. When you eat a small bowl of steel-cut oats or a slice of dense, seeded bread, the complex carbohydrates break down slowly. Glucose enters the bloodstream at a measured pace, providing steady fuel for the brain and muscles rather than a jolt followed by a crash. The fiber also feeds the gut microbiome, producing short-chain fatty acids that reduce inflammation and support immune function. In short, whole grains deliver the sustained satisfaction that a bag of pretzels simply cannot replicate.

Legumes complement this picture with an equally impressive profile. Beans, lentils, chickpeas, and peas bring together the two nutrients most lacking in processed snacks: protein and fiber. A cup of cooked lentils contains roughly eighteen grams of protein and sixteen grams of fiber, along with substantial amounts of iron, folate, and potassium. This combination slows gastric emptying and triggers satiety hormones that tell the brain, calmly and clearly, that the body has been fed. Roasted chickpeas seasoned with cumin, a small container of lentil salad dressed with lemon and olive oil, or even a spoonful of almond butter on whole-grain crackers can silence hunger for hours. Compare that to the hollow fullness of cheese puffs, which vanish within minutes and demand more.

Making the transition does not require an austere overhaul of your pantry. Start by placing a jar of cooked quinoa or farro in the refrigerator where the cookie tin used to sit. Keep roasted edamame or homemade hummus within arm’s reach. When the afternoon slump arrives, reach for something that requires a little chewing and offers genuine texture. Your blood sugar will remain steadier, your concentration sharper, and your cravings quieter. Over weeks, the palate adjusts. Foods once dismissed as bland begin to taste nuanced, while the hyper-salted, hyper-sweet profiles of processed snacks start to feel almost aggressive.

Choosing whole grains and legumes over packaged snacks is less about restriction and more about upgrading the quality of your fuel. It is a quiet revolution in how you eat, one that honors your body’s need for real nourishment in the small moments between meals. The snack drawer need not be a place of surrender. With a little foresight, it can become a source of genuine sustenance.

title: teaching memoir|a first year teaching in an underfunded high school
text:
Room 214

I was hired over the phone, nine days before school started, to teach English at Hollis High, home of the Ironworkers—though the ironworks closed in 2011 and the mascot had long since become a civic joke. Salary: $35,800. Room: 214, which had thirty-one desks, a whiteboard that ghosted everything ever written on it, and a ceiling tile stained the exact shape of Lake Superior. I had five sections and 164 students. I was twenty-three and had tabbed my copy of the state standards like scripture.

The veterans ran a betting pool on when I'd cry. Darlene, across the hall, twenty-seven years in, told me this with pride, like a tradition. She had her money on Halloween. "Everybody cries by Halloween," she said, "or they aren't paying attention."

October: the copier died for eleven days, and I learned the building actually ran on a woman named Miss Betty in the front office, who had a personal machine, a sign-in sheet, and the air of a border crossing. I learned a "class set" of *Monster* by Walter Dean Myers meant twenty-two copies for thirty-four kids, so we read in trios, which the students called book jail. I learned the heater in 214 had two settings—off, and the surface of the sun—and that a blazer was a rookie mistake. I spent $600 of my own money by Christmas and called it an investment, which is what you say when you're twenty-three.

Jaylin ran a store out of his backpack. Chips, phone chargers, once a single glove. I confiscated the inventory in November and found, under the Takis, a composition notebook with a ledger: names, debts, due dates, a column labeled "interest." He charged interest. I gave it back. The math was right.

In March, a girl named Tamia, who had said maybe forty words to me all year, filled two pages of margins in *Monster* arguing about whether Steve Harmon was lying. Tiny, furious handwriting. I wrote back. We kept a correspondence going in that paperback for six weeks, and I never told her it was the best writing conference I had all year by a mile.

I did not cry by Halloween. I cried on April 12th, in my car, in the parking lot, heat blasting because the knob had broken that way. Darlene knocked on the window and handed me a gas-station coffee. She didn't say anything wise. She said, "There's no ahead, baby. There's just the room," and went back inside.

In May, Tamia asked if she could keep the book. It was school property—one of twenty-two copies for thirty-four kids, and I knew exactly which trios would be short next fall.

She kept the book.

title: healthy eating guide|why whole grains and legumes should replace processed snacks
text:
Chapter 6: Make the Default Snack Do More

At four o’clock, when my energy dips and dinner still feels far away, I don’t want a lecture on nutrition. I want something convenient and satisfying. That is precisely why the snack choice matters: it is often made quickly, repeatedly, and under the influence of hunger. I’ve found it more useful to change my default option than to rely on willpower.

For many people, the default is chips, sweets, pastries, or refined-flour crackers. Processing itself is not the enemy—canned beans, frozen vegetables, and whole-grain bread are processed foods too. The concern is a pattern of snacking on products that supply plenty of refined starch, added sugar, sodium, or fat, but relatively little fiber or protein. They can be easy to eat quickly and still leave me looking for something else soon afterward. There is no moral failure in enjoying them; there is simply an opportunity to make the everyday choice more nourishing.

Whole grains and legumes are especially useful replacements because they bring substance, not just calories. A whole grain retains its bran, germ, and endosperm. Oats, brown rice, barley, quinoa, whole wheat, and plain popcorn all count. Legumes include lentils, chickpeas, black beans, kidney beans, split peas, and edamame. Depending on the food and serving, they offer combinations of fiber, plant protein, B vitamins, folate, magnesium, potassium, and iron.

Fiber is central to their advantage. It adds bulk, slows eating, and helps a snack feel more substantial. Protein contributes to satisfaction as well. A bowl of lentil soup or whole-grain toast with hummus usually stays with me longer than a handful of refined crackers. For many people, pairing fiber and protein also produces a gentler rise in blood glucose than a similarly sized serving of sweets or refined starch, although individual responses and portions vary. Fiber additionally supports digestive health and provides fuel for beneficial gut bacteria.

 Make the swap practical

I don’t ask myself to snack on a plain scoop of brown rice. The replacement has to compete on flavor and convenience. I might keep cooked chickpeas in the refrigerator for a quick lemon-and-herb dip, spread hummus on whole-grain toast, or season air-popped popcorn and pair it with a handful of edamame. Overnight oats can become an afternoon snack, and leftover black beans can fill a small whole-grain tortilla with salsa. Roasted chickpeas offer crunch; white-bean dip offers the creamy texture I might otherwise seek from a packaged snack.

Preparation does not have to mean hours of cooking. Canned legumes are affordable and fast, and rinsing them reduces some of the sodium. Low-sodium options are useful when available. A batch of lentils can be cooked once, refrigerated for several days, or frozen in portions. Oats, popcorn kernels, and dried beans store well. When buying bread or crackers, I look beyond brown coloring and words such as “multigrain”: I check that a whole grain appears first in the ingredient list and compare the fiber and sodium per serving.

The most sustainable approach is gradual. If your current diet is low in fiber, suddenly adding large amounts of beans and bran may cause gas or discomfort. Start with modest portions, increase them over time, and drink enough fluid. It also helps to replace one snack at a time rather than declaring the entire pantry off-limits. A chickpea dip you enjoy is a better plan than a “perfect” snack you never eat.

My own rule is simple: make whole grains and legumes the foundation of most snacks, then add flavor and pleasure. Sometimes that means cinnamon in oats, smoked paprika on popcorn, or garlic in bean dip. Sometimes it means having the packaged treat because I genuinely want it—not because it was the only thing within reach.

The goal is not a life without convenience foods or indulgence. It is to stop asking processed snacks to do a job they often do poorly: keeping us satisfied while contributing meaningful nutrition. Whole grains and legumes can do that job, affordably and deliciously. When they become the easy default, better snacking depends less on restraint and more on a kitchen that is working with you.

title: Very Short Introduction-style book|the history and ideas of the Enlightenment
text:
The Enlightenment is usually associated with eighteenth-century Europe, but it is better understood as a changing set of arguments than as a single movement. Its participants disagreed about religion, government, human nature, and even the powers of reason. What connected them was a conviction that inherited beliefs and institutions should be examined, and that knowledge could improve human life. In 1784 Immanuel Kant described enlightenment as emergence from “self-incurred immaturity” and gave it the motto sapere aude: “dare to know.”

Its intellectual origins lay partly in the Scientific Revolution. Copernicus, Galileo, and Newton had made nature seem intelligible through observation and mathematics, while offering powerful examples of established authority being revised. John Locke presented the mind as shaped by experience and defended religious toleration; Spinoza and Pierre Bayle supplied more unsettling challenges to biblical and ecclesiastical authority. European states were also being transformed by commerce, overseas empire, and memories of religious war. These developments did not make tradition disappear. They gave critics new standards by which to judge it.

Enlightenment was also a social practice. Its ideas circulated through books, periodicals, correspondence, academies, coffeehouses, and salons, often across linguistic and political borders. Censorship encouraged coded language, anonymous publication, and a vigorous trade in forbidden works. In France, the philosophes formed no unified party, but many shared projects of criticism and reform. The Encyclopédie, edited by Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d’Alembert, gathered contributions on theology, politics, crafts, and science. It was at once a reference work, a commercial venture, and an attempt to show how knowledge was made and how it might be used.

Reason did not mean cold calculation alone. Thinkers investigated sensation, emotion, sociability, and imagination; David Hume, indeed, was as interested in the limits of reason as in its powers. Montesquieu compared laws and political institutions, Rousseau asked whether social inequality corrupted natural human capacities, and Adam Smith examined how markets and moral sentiments bound people together. Across these inquiries ran a new interest in history as human development. “Progress” became both a hope and a disputed claim, not a guaranteed law of history.

Religion remained central. Few philosophes were straightforward atheists; many were deists, sceptics, or reforming Christians. The central issue was often not belief itself but the coercive power of churches and states. Demands for toleration and freedom of expression could coexist with confidence in strong monarchy, and rulers such as Frederick II of Prussia and Catherine II of Russia adopted Enlightenment language while preserving autocracy. The American and French Revolutions drew on ideas of rights, representation, and popular sovereignty, but neither simply enacted a ready-made Enlightenment programme.

Universal claims were often narrower in practice. Women, labourers, enslaved people, and colonized populations were frequently excluded from full membership in the human community whose reason and rights philosophers celebrated. Some writers attacked slavery; others defended racial hierarchies or benefited from colonial commerce. Women nevertheless shaped the movement as salon hosts, translators, and authors. Mary Wollstonecraft turned arguments about natural rights against female subordination, while the Haitian Revolution, made by enslaved and formerly enslaved people, exposed the limits of European universalism by demanding liberty and equality in fact.

The Enlightenment’s legacy is therefore double-sided but not simply contradictory. It helped to shape modern ideals of human rights, secular government, scientific inquiry, and public criticism, while its confidence in classification and mastery could also serve empire and social control. Later admirers and critics have alternately treated it as the source of modern freedom or of modern domination. To study it is not to choose once and for all between celebration and condemnation. It is to see how arguments about knowledge, freedom, equality, and authority emerged together, and why their tensions remain familiar.

title: biography|a nineteenth-century woman astronomer
text:
Williamina Fleming began her working life in Dundee, Scotland, fetching water for a family of eight and ended it bent over glass photographic plates in a drafty Cambridge annex, mapping the heavens. In between, she catalogued ten thousand stars, named dozens of novae, and discovered the Horsehead Nebula almost as an afterthought.

She arrived in Boston in 1878, twenty-one years old, pregnant, and married to a man who would soon vanish from the record. By 1881 she was scrubbing floors for Edward Charles Pickering, director of the Harvard College Observatory. The story goes that one autumn afternoon Pickering burst from the computing room in disgust, claiming that even his Scottish maid could sort stellar spectra better than his bored Harvard undergraduates. Whether the tantrum happened beside a mop bucket or over a supper table, Pickering hired Fleming that October at wages scarcely better than domestic service. She traded housework for a desk in the brick annex on Garden Street, and the observatory’s ambitions shifted overnight.

Fleming’s eyes were extraordinary, but her discipline was industrial. During the next three decades she examined tens of thousands of glass negatives shipped back from telescopes in Cambridge and at the remote station in Arequipa, Peru. In 1888 she was flipping through a plate of Orion’s belt when she noticed a murky intrusion in the gas and dust—a phantom shaped like a chess knight’s head. She logged it simply as “large nebulosity,” but astronomers later christened it the Horsehead. She also identified fifty-nine gaseous nebulae, over three hundred variable stars, and ten novae, all while raising her son, Edward, on a salary that peaked at fifteen hundred dollars a year. Respectable for a woman in 1890, perhaps, but roughly half what a male assistant earned for lighter output.

Her greatest labor was the *Draper Catalogue of Stellar Spectra*, published in 1890, which arranged more than ten thousand stars according to the strength of their hydrogen lines. Fleming devised an alphabetical scheme—A, B, C, and downward—that her colleague Annie Jump Cannon later refined into the famous O-B-A-F-G-K-M sequence. For years Fleming served as curator of astronomical photographs, effectively supervising the observatory’s growing colony of female “computers.” In 1906 the Royal Astronomical Society of London made her an honorary member, the first American woman so recognized. She wore the honor with characteristic practicality; by then she was running the photographic department, publishing under her own name in the *Astrophysical Journal*, and quietly fuming that her title remained “computer” while men with fewer discoveries were called astronomers.

She died of pneumonia in the winter of 1911, aged fifty-four, leaving behind a drawer of handwritten notebooks and a son who had watched his mother classify the universe from a salary ledger. The Horsehead still stands in Orion, dark against the glow, because a former housekeeper in Cambridge had the patience to notice a shadow.

title: how-to guide for aspiring authors|outlining a non-fiction book before writing the first draft
text:
Start with the book’s promise, not its table of contents. In one or two sentences, name the reader, the problem, and the useful change the book will deliver. “A book about productivity” is a topic; “a guide that helps freelancers plan realistic weeks without working every weekend” is a promise. Keep this statement where you can see it. Every chapter, story, and digression should either advance that promise or justify its place.

Next, define the reader’s starting point and the limits of your scope. What does your audience already know, fear, or misunderstand? What will you assume rather than explain? Write a short “not in this book” list as well; it prevents a focused guide from swelling into an encyclopedia. If you are writing memoir-driven or narrative nonfiction, apply the same discipline by identifying the central question and the experiences or evidence needed to explore it.

Choose an organizing principle that suits the promise. Common options include chronological development, a step-by-step process, problems paired with solutions, major themes, or a sequence of questions. Draft a working table of contents, then add one sentence beneath each chapter title describing its job. Use verbs such as explain, challenge, demonstrate, or equip. A strong sequence creates momentum: each chapter resolves something important while making the next chapter necessary.

Expand each chapter into a compact brief. Include its central claim, the question it answers, three to five essential points, supporting examples or evidence, and the takeaway you want readers to remember. Note any exercise, story, case study, or transition that belongs there. Keep this brief separate from your research notes. The outline should show the chapter’s argument and shape, not contain every quotation and fact you might eventually use.

Audit the outline for research gaps before drafting. Mark claims that need sources, stories that require interviews, and examples that still need verification. Distinguish what you must find from what would merely be nice to have, and flag material that may require permission. This audit gives research a purpose and exposes weak chapters early. Set a stopping rule, too: exhaustive research can become a respectable way to avoid making decisions on the page.

Now test the structure. Read only the chapter titles and summaries, as if you were browsing the book. Look for repeated ideas, missing prerequisites, abrupt leaps, and chapters that seem to belong to another project. Check balance as well. If one chapter carries half the book’s substance, divide it; if another has only a single observation, fold it elsewhere. A rough word budget for each chapter can reveal these problems and make the total project feel manageable.

If possible, test the sequence on a few members of your intended audience. Ask what they would expect to learn, where they would feel lost, and which chapter they would read first. Their answers can expose assumptions that are invisible when you know the subject too well.

Treat the outline as a working hypothesis rather than a contract. Drafting will reveal better examples, unexpected objections, and connections you could not see in advance. When the plan changes, revise the chapter summaries so the outline remains a trustworthy map. Keep a separate parking lot for attractive but nonessential ideas; this lets you preserve them without allowing them to distort the book’s argument.

Stop outlining when you can explain, without notes, why the book matters, how the chapters fit together, and what each chapter must accomplish. More detail will not guarantee an easier draft, and excessive planning can make the prose feel preassembled. Choose a chapter you understand well—often not the introduction—and draft toward its stated outcome. Your aim before writing is not certainty. It is a clear route, visible gaps, and enough freedom to discover better answers along the way.

title: food-politics book|how industrial agriculture shapes what ends up on our plates
text:
A boneless chicken breast looks like the end of a story. In fact, it is the visible tip of a system whose other parts are kept conveniently out of view: the genetics company that bred the bird, the grain markets that priced its feed, the lender that financed the grower’s sheds, the processor that set the line speed, and the retailer that decided what an acceptable portion should cost. Long before a shopper chooses dinner, a chain of institutions has narrowed the choices available.

Industrial agriculture is often pictured as a landscape of vast fields and enormous machines. It is also a way of organizing time, risk, and taste. Crops are selected for yield, uniformity, and their ability to survive transport; animals are raised to reach market weight quickly; food is designed to fit warehouses, delivery schedules, and standardized kitchens. These achievements are real. So is the abundance they make possible. But efficiency is never neutral. Every gain answers a question about what should be optimized, and every answer favors some eater, worker, or business over another.

In the United States, for example, farm policy has historically done more to secure supplies of certain commodity crops than to determine what a balanced diet should look like. Corn and soybeans move through the system as animal feed, sweeteners, oils, and industrial ingredients, becoming almost invisible by the time they reach the plate. Their apparent cheapness helps shape the price of meat, snacks, and packaged meals. Meanwhile, costs that do not appear at the checkout—eroded soil, polluted water, injured workers, depleted aquifers—are transferred to rural communities, future taxpayers, and people with the least power to refuse them.

The supermarket then translates this arrangement into the language of personal preference. A flawless tomato may have been bred less for fragrance than for firmness; a chicken’s portion size may reflect processing requirements as much as appetite; a breakfast cereal may turn subsidized grain and sophisticated marketing into a morning ritual. None of this requires a secret committee deciding what families should eat. It requires only thousands of reasonable decisions, each made within a system that rewards scale and punishes deviation.

Nor is the alternative a simple return to an imagined pastoral past. Small farms can exploit workers, local food can carry a premium that excludes the poor, and year-round plenty is not a blessing to mock. For households counting every dollar, the industrial plate can be a source of security as well as frustration. The political task is not to make people feel guilty for buying what is affordable. It is to ask why affordability so often depends on hidden damage, and why the foods most compatible with public health are frequently treated as specialty goods.

Changing what we eat therefore means changing more than individual habits. Public procurement can create dependable markets for different crops. Research budgets can support varieties chosen for resilience and flavor, not only transportability. Labor law can make a cheap meal less dependent on cheapening the people who produce it. Competition policy can give farmers and independent processors room to survive. None of these measures fits neatly on a label, which is precisely why labels have absorbed so much of our attention.

A plate is not a ballot, and dinner cannot carry the whole burden of reform. Yet it is a record of decisions made elsewhere, often in our name. To read that record is to see that the opposite of industrial food is not simply artisanal food. It is a food system in which efficiency is judged alongside health, dignity, and ecological survival—and in which the people asked to live with the consequences have some say in the menu.

title: how-to guide for aspiring authors|outlining a non-fiction book before writing the first draft
text:
Chapter 4: The Road-Tested Outline

I learned the hard way that enthusiasm is not a structure. Five years ago, I sat down to write my first non-fiction book armed with little more than a title I loved and a burning conviction that I had something important to say. Thirty thousand words later, I had a graveyard of half-developed ideas, three separate introductions, and a chapter on research methodology that somehow morphed into a memoir about my childhood dog. None of it cohered. The manuscript didn’t need an editor; it needed an exorcist. The problem wasn’t my subject or my sentence-level skill—it was that I had tried to build a house by decorating rooms before pouring the foundation. I had confused knowing *about* a topic with knowing *how to teach* it.

Non-fiction is not a journey of discovery for the writer in the same way fiction can be. Your reader is paying you for clarity, for a promised transformation, and for a logical path from confusion to understanding. That path must exist before you type “Chapter One.” This is why I now spend nearly as long outlining as I do drafting. The outline is the book’s first draft; the prose is merely the second.

Here is the three-tier method I use now, and the one I recommend to every aspiring author before they write a single scene.

Tier One: The Contract
Start with a single page. Define the promise of your book in one sentence: *When the reader finishes this book, they will be able to ______ because they will understand ______.* If you cannot fill in those blanks, you are not ready to outline; you are still brainstorming. Beneath that promise, draft a working table of contents with no more than twelve to fifteen chapters. I force this limit because constraint breeds creativity. If you genuinely need twenty chapters, you are likely writing two books. Each chapter title should read like a stepping stone toward your promise, not a miscellaneous container for a topic you find interesting.

Tier Two: The Chapter Summary
Once your table of contents feels inevitable—like you are merely describing a structure that already exists—expand each chapter into a three-to-five-sentence summary. State the chapter’s core argument, the specific evidence or story you will use to support it, and the transition that hands the reader off to the next chapter. If a chapter summary cannot answer *why this chapter must come here and not there*, reorder your table of contents until the sequence feels causal, not just chronological. I write these summaries in a single running document and read them aloud in one sitting. If I bore myself, I have identified a flat stretch of road before I have wasted weeks paving it. If a transition feels forced, I know I am relying on clever segues instead of genuine logic.

Tier Three: The Beats
Only now do you zoom in. For each chapter, create a bullet-point list of every section, anecdote, data point, and takeaway. I call these “beats,” borrowed from screenwriting, because they dictate rhythm. A typical non-fiction chapter of four thousand words might have eight to twelve beats. One beat might be: *Open with the 2018 MIT study on decision fatigue—connect to morning routines—segue to the “choice audit” exercise.* This is not prose; it is architecture. You are deciding where the load-bearing walls go before you choose the paint color.

Here is the final test I apply before I call an outline finished. I set it aside for forty-eight hours—minimum—then return and read only the chapter summaries, one after another, as if they were a stand-alone mini-book. Does the logic hold? Does curiosity escalate? If a stranger read these two pages, would they feel the full shape of the argument and trust that the author knows where they are going? If the answer is no, I revise the summaries until they sing in harmony. Only then, and only when I can see the whole book in my mind’s eye, do I open a blank document for Chapter One.

I must say this plainly: your outline is not a prison. I deviate from my beats constantly while drafting. A new study appears; an interview subject offers a better anecdote than the one I planned; a chapter argues back and demands more space. The outline gives you permission to deviate intelligently. When you feel the pull to wander, you can look at your roadmap and ask, *Does this detour serve the promise, or am I just chasing the dog from my childhood again?*

When the outline is solid, the writing becomes execution instead of invention. You are no longer staring into the void; you are filling a form. For non-fiction authors, that distinction is the difference between a manuscript that gets finished and one that joins the graveyard.

title: memoir|a diplomat's first posting abroad during the Cold War
text:
I arrived in Moscow on a wet October evening in 1961, twenty-four years old and carrying, in a leather briefcase my father had given me, nothing more classified than a change of shirts and a letter of introduction to the ambassador. The airport smelled of coal smoke and wet wool. A man from the embassy met me and drove me through streets so wide and empty they seemed designed for parades that had been cancelled.

My flat was on the sixth floor of a foreigners' compound near the river, with high ceilings, a tile stove, and windows that faced a courtyard where the same black Volga was parked every morning, its driver pretending to read a newspaper. We were told to assume the rooms listened. I developed the habit, which I have never entirely lost, of saying anything important out of doors.

The embassy was a small world unto itself, and I was its smallest inhabitant. Third secretaries did the work no one else wanted: drafting condolence letters, counting heads at receptions, standing in line at the Intourist office for tickets to the Bolshoi so that the counsellor's wife could take her visiting sister. I did not mind. I was young, and Moscow at twenty-four is an education no university could offer. I learned to drink vodka without grimacing. I learned that a Russian's "no" could mean "perhaps" and his "perhaps" could mean "never." I learned to skate badly on the rink at Gorky Park while girls in fur hats glided past me like swans.

The man who read his newspaper in the courtyard was, I came to understand, mine. My shadow. Everyone had one. Ours was a civil arrangement; if I left the compound on foot he followed at a polite distance, and once, when I lost my way in the back streets beyond the Arbat, he materialized at my elbow and pointed me home without a word. I never learned his name. I have wondered, in the decades since, what became of him, whether he filed reports on a young man whose only secrets were his wretched Russian grammar and his homesickness.

Then came October of 1962, and the world held its breath. I remember the embassy basement, the burn bags, the cipher clerks working through the night. I remember walking to the office past queues at the bread shops that were longer than usual, and the strange stillness of the streets, as if the whole city were listening to a radio I could not hear. The ambassador, a veteran of worse crises, told us to stay calm and carry on with our duties, and so I stood at a reception that week watching a Soviet deputy minister toast "peaceful coexistence" with a smile that did not reach his eyes, and I understood for the first time that the phrase was not a hope but a threat wrapped in courtesy.

When it ended, when the ships turned around, I went out onto the street and breathed the cold air like a man surfacing from deep water. I was alive, and the world was intact, and I was too young to know how close it had been.

I stayed three years. Moscow made me a diplomat; it taught me that nations are abstractions but people are not, that the man in the Volga had a family, that the deputy minister's smile hid fear as much as menace. We were enemies by profession and neighbors by geography. I have spent the rest of my career trying to remember both halves of that sentence, and the rest of my life failing, most days, to say it well.

title: memoir|a playwright's early years of failure in New York
text:
The first play of mine produced in New York ran for four performances, though “produced” may be too generous a word. A director I had met while waiting tables rented the basement of a church on West Seventy-Fourth Street for two hundred dollars and my promise to repaint the dressing room. We borrowed forty chairs from a funeral home. On opening night, twenty-six people came, nine of them related to the cast. I sat in the back with my coat on, ready to leave if the applause became unbearable.

I had arrived two years earlier, at twenty-four, with a duffel bag, a Smith-Corona, and the belief that failure would be brief and instructive. I shared a railroad flat near Tompkins Square with an actor who auditioned for commercials and a dancer who seldom came home. My own room was wide enough for a mattress if I kept the door open. During the day I typed insurance policies; on weekends I waited tables; late at night I wrote plays in which people said the things I had been too frightened or too slow to say myself.

The city offered a steady supply of almost. A literary manager requested a script and kept it for eight months. An agent praised my work over lunch, then moved to Los Angeles without leaving an address. Once, a famous actress telephoned to say she loved a play of mine. I sat beside the phone for three evenings afterward, as if her regard required supervision. When my father asked how things were going, I spoke about readings and workshops, never mentioning that attendance at either was often optional.

My church-basement play was called The Winter Room, a title I now remember with slight embarrassment. It concerned a young man, an old woman, and a great deal of symbolic weather. A reviewer for a downtown weekly wrote that it seemed to have been written by someone who had overheard life but not yet lived it. I hated him for the precision of the sentence. I had thought suffering in proximity to art was the same as having something to say.

After the final performance, we folded the funeral-home chairs and stacked them by the door. The actress playing the old woman, who was twenty-nine, cried because she had nowhere else to go that winter. I wanted someone to tell me to stop. No one did. Failure in New York was rarely dramatic. Doors did not slam; they remained politely open onto rooms you could not afford to enter. Mostly, the telephone did not ring, and the rent arrived with perfect regularity.

I kept writing, though not out of the clean courage people later like to attribute to the young. I stayed because I did not know who else to be, and because, on certain mornings, a sentence would surprise me. That was enough to get me to the next sentence. Slowly, I began listening to the customers at the restaurant, to my roommate practicing sincerity for soap commercials, to the silence after my father asked whether I was eating properly. I put less weather in my plays. They did not improve at once, but they became less concerned with my wish to be admired.

Years later, when people asked how I endured those years, I was tempted to describe perseverance, as if I had possessed a plan. What I had was a habit, indistinguishable at times from stubbornness or fear. Still, habits can carry a person where confidence cannot. The city had not been testing me. It had simply been going on without me, and there was a strange freedom in that. I stopped writing for the people who might discover me and began writing for the strangers in those borrowed chairs.

title: popular science book|how the immune system learns to recognise invaders
text:
The most consequential drop of pus in medical history passed, on 14 May 1796, from a milkmaid to a small boy. Edward Jenner took material from a cowpox sore on Sarah Nelmes’s hand and scratched it into the arm of eight-year-old James Phipps. The boy became mildly ill, recovered, and later failed to develop smallpox when Jenner exposed him to material from a smallpox sore. No ethics committee would sanction the experiment today. Yet it revealed something uncanny: the body can be taught to recognise an enemy without first being nearly killed by it.

That teaching is done by the adaptive immune system, and its first trick is not memory but extravagant guesswork.

Long before you meet a virus, your body has been manufacturing lymphocytes with different receptors. Rather than keep a finished receptor for every possible microbe, each developing B or T cell shuffles gene segments—the biological equivalent of cutting up a pack of cards and dealing itself a new hand. The theoretical variety runs into the trillions. Many guesses are useless. Some are dangerous: in the thymus, T cells that react too strongly to the body’s own tissues are mostly destroyed. Learning to recognise invaders begins with learning what not to attack.

When infection arrives, a dendritic cell behaves less like a soldier than a forensic officer with a taste for display. It engulfs debris, chops proteins into peptides and presents them on molecular platforms called MHC. A T cell whose receptor fits one peptide–MHC combination can stop and listen—provided other signals confirm that this is danger, not harmless rubbish. Then comes the audacious part: that one cell divides. A rare guess becomes a clone. Helper T cells coordinate the response; killer T cells destroy infected cells displaying the same evidence.

B cells work differently, often binding intact molecules on an invader’s surface. With help from T cells, the successful ones multiply and can become plasma cells, each able to release roughly 2,000 antibody molecules a second. Nor is the first draft final. In germinal centres—temporary training camps inside lymph nodes and the spleen—B cells mutate their antibody genes and compete. Cells that bind more tightly prosper; poorer binders disappear. The immune system does not simply remember. It edits.

Once the emergency passes, most of this army dies. A residue remains: memory B and T cells, plus antibodies that may circulate for years. On a second encounter, recognition is quicker and the response larger and often better aimed. This is why a second infection may be stopped before you notice it, and why vaccination works. A vaccine supplies the lesson—an antigen, or instructions for making one—without requiring the full disease.

Jenner knew nothing of lymphocytes. But cowpox gave James Phipps’s immune system a sketch close enough to smallpox to be useful. That is the deep cunning of immunity: it cannot foresee every enemy, so it generates absurd diversity, selects what fits, sharpens the fit, and keeps the notes. Not a wall, then, but a wanted poster revised in pencil—and, when necessary, in blood.

title: memoir|growing up in a small mining town in the 1960s
text:
We woke to the whistle at five, a sound that carried through the hollow like a wounded bird. My father was already up, sitting at the kitchen table in his union suit, the kerosene lamp throwing shadows across the wallpaper my mother had pasted with flour paste. Outside, the headframe of Number 7 shaft stood black against a sky just beginning to gray above the eastern ridge. On damp mornings you could smell the tipple, a sharp sulfurous tang that settled in your throat and never quite left.

Our street ran parallel to the creek, twelve company houses painted identical shades of pale green or cream, depending on what the company store had surplus. Mrs. DeWitt next door kept chickens behind her coal shed, and in summer the smell of their feed mixed with the honeysuckle on her fence. The creek ran orange, stained by acid drainage that no one discussed because the mine was the reason we ate.

I was ten in 1963, old enough to know that black lung had taken my grandfather before I was born, old enough to understand why my mother cried into her dishrag when the afternoon shift ran late. The men came home with rings of grime around their necks that no amount of Lava soap could remove. My father’s hands were scarred and thickened, the nails split and blue-tinged from injuries he never discussed. On payday Fridays he walked to the company store with his check already spent in his mind.

The school was a two-story brick building with a coal furnace that the janitor stoked beginning at four in the morning. In winter we lined our galoshes along the radiator and watched snow fall past frosted windows, each of us knowing without saying which boys would follow their fathers underground and which would leave on the Greyhound bus that stopped twice daily outside the diner. I wanted to believe I would be a leaver, though I could not imagine what lay beyond the ridges that cupped our town like hands.

Sundays belonged to church and visiting. After Mass at St. Michael’s, families walked down Main Street, the women in hats despite the heat, the men in clean shirts showing permanent creases from work clothes folded too long in drawers. We visited my mother’s sister, who lived nearer the tipple where vibrations from coal cars rattled dishes in her cabinets. The women talked in the kitchen over percolated coffee while the men sat on the porch, smoking and saying little, watching the mountain.

There was a violence to life there that we accepted. The mine took fingers, lungs, sometimes whole men. When the siren wailed in midday, the town held its breath. Women came to their porches with dish towels in hand, looking toward the shaft. We children stopped our games and waited. No one needed to explain what the long wail meant versus the short bursts. We knew the vocabulary of disaster before we knew the vocabulary of hope.

By the end of the decade, the seams were thinning and talk turned to closure. The company store stocked less, shelves growing patchy. My father mentioned automobile plants in Ohio, relatives in Akron who said there was work. The whistle blew less often. When it finally stopped in 1969, the silence was so profound that people complained they could not sleep. We had grown accustomed to the noise, to the groaning of the earth being emptied beneath us, to the sense that something large was happening just out of sight.

I left for college in 1971, the first in my family. When I go back now, the headframe is rusted and the company houses stand vacant, windows like blind eyes. The creek still runs orange. But sometimes, standing where our kitchen used to be, I hear that five o’clock whistle and smell my father’s lamp oil, and I am a child again in a place that no longer exists except in the bones of the mountain and the memory of those who stayed.

title: food-politics book|how industrial agriculture shapes what ends up on our plates
text:
The Invisible Architects of Dinner

Most of us believe that we choose what we eat. We push our carts through the fluorescent aisles, comparing prices, scanning labels, surrendering to the occasional craving. It feels like freedom, this abundance, and in a narrow sense it is. But the supermarket is a landscape that was surveyed long before we arrived, drawn up in congressional hearing rooms, in the greenhouses of seed companies, in the trading pits where grain futures change hands. By the time a product reaches the shelf, the decisive choices about it have already been made, and they were not made by eaters.

Consider corn. For half a century, American farm policy has rewarded farmers for producing as much of it as possible, along with its companion crop, soybeans. Subsidies, crop insurance, and the quiet architecture of the Farm Bill push land toward monoculture, and monoculture pushes back with its own logic: bigger machinery, more chemical fertilizer, fewer farmers on fewer, larger farms. The result is a river of cheap grain, far more than the nation could ever eat in recognizable form. Something had to be done with all that surplus, and the food industry rose to the task with great ingenuity.

Some of the river flows into feedlots, where cattle designed by nature to eat grass are fattened on corn instead, their stomachs medicated to tolerate a diet evolution never intended. Cheap grain made cheap meat, and cheap meat remade the national diet: the hamburger became an everyday food rather than an occasional one. Some of the river flows into factories, where corn is disassembled into sweeteners and starches and oils, then reassembled into the soft drinks, snacks, and frozen dinners that fill the center aisles of the store. This is why a dollar buys more calories of potato chips than of broccoli. Not because chips are natural or inevitable, but because decades of policy made their raw ingredients artificially cheap while fruits and vegetables received a fraction of the support.

Nor is the shaping only economic. A handful of corporations now control most of the world's commercial seed supply; four companies slaughter most of America's beef; a single firm may decide, by changing one recipe, the fate of an entire harvest. These companies employ lobbyists who help write the farm bills and scientists who help draft the dietary guidelines, so that the advice we receive about eating is itself partly an industry product. Even the supermarket layout is a form of governance: the profitable processed goods at eye level, the perimeter of perishables arranged to suggest freshness and virtue.

None of this is a conspiracy. It is a system, and systems have momentum. The farmer on the tractor, the worker on the packing line, the parent doing the weekly shopping, all are responding rationally to incentives built by others. That is precisely the point. When we are told that obesity and diabetes are matters of personal responsibility, we should ask who built the environment in which those responsibilities must be exercised. The industrial food chain did not merely supply our appetites; it educated them, cheapened some foods and made others dear, and narrowed the meaning of choice until it fit within a package. The costs that never appear on the receipt, the eroded soil, the antibiotic losing its power, the shuttered main street of a farm town, are quietly paid elsewhere, by everyone.

What ends up on our plates, then, is not simply what we want. It is what the system wants, disguised as what we want. To eat thoughtfully is not to retreat into purity, but to recognize the plate as the last stop on a long political journey, and to begin, perhaps, asking for a different itinerary.

title: journalism / narrative non-fiction|a town's struggle after its only factory closes
text:
The Payroll Left Town

GIDEON, Ohio — The last thing Ray Dobbs made at Gideon Implement was a latch for a feed wagon. He stamped it, brushed off the burr and laid it beside 11,943 others. Then he wiped his press with a blue rag he had carried, washed and carried again for nearly 20 years.

It was 2:17 p.m. on March 28. Dobbs, 56, had worked there 32 years. The company gave him a cardboard box for his tools and a pamphlet about continuing his health insurance. Nobody made a speech. By 3:04, the parking lot was empty except for a crow working over a French fry.

For 71 years, Gideon’s only factory had made feed wagons and, later, parts for other people’s machines. It survived two fires, the farm crisis and an owner who briefly insisted on painting every press turquoise. It did not survive a consolidation plan drawn up in Schaumburg, Illinois. Halloran Ag Systems, which bought the plant in 2016, moved the work to Missouri. In its announcement, “Gideon” appeared once; “synergies” appeared twice.

The closure took 386 jobs from a town of 2,408. In 1992, there had been 817. The final payroll was $16.4 million, in a place where the dollar-store cashier knows which customers are waiting until Friday to buy dog food.

Noma Velez, owner of the Coffee Cup on Water Street, used to serve 90 breakfasts before first shift. On a Tuesday in June, she served 31. She stopped ordering pie on Thursdays and cut her daughter’s hours, neither of which appears in the state’s monthly employment report.

At village hall, Mayor Linda Orr keeps a composition notebook with three columns: DUE, OVERDUE and WAIT. The factory was the water system’s largest customer; its $19,000 monthly bill is gone. Gideon has postponed an $84,000 repair to the north water tower and left two streets department jobs unfilled.

“Everybody wants a ribbon-cutting,” Orr said. “I’d settle for somebody who needs 40,000 gallons of water a day.”

The state sent a rapid-response team and a flyer about welding classes. The classes are in Mansfield, 38 miles away, on Tuesday and Thursday nights. Dobbs went twice. Then he took a job at a distribution center 43 miles in the other direction. It pays $18.25 an hour; he made $26.40 at the plant. He leaves home at 4:50 a.m. and buys fuel by the twenty, not by the tank.

At the library, a contractor helped 14 former employees write résumés. She changed Dobbs’s “press operator” to “manufacturing associate.” He changed it back.

By August, 23 children had withdrawn from Gideon’s schools. The Lutheran church combined its two Sunday services. The factory’s buyer has not materialized, though a broker from Columbus did tour the building and ask whether the roof leaked. It does, Orr told him, mostly over the old tool room.

Dobbs still carries his time card in his truck’s visor. Not for sentiment, he said. The clip is broken, and the card keeps his registration from falling out.

title: memoir|a playwright's early years of failure in New York
text:
Chapter Four: The House Lights

Failure in New York did not announce itself. It did not slam a door or tell me to go home. It said, *Thank you for your interest.* It said, *We received an unusually large number of submissions.* Then it asked whether I could cover a shift on Saturday.

I was twenty-three when I arrived with two suitcases, $1,600, and a play called *Winter Arithmetic*. The play was ninety-two pages long and concerned, as far as I can now determine, a family standing in various kitchens refusing to say what they meant. I mistook its obscurity for depth. I had read that New York rewarded nerve, so I quit my job at a bank in Columbus and took a room in Astoria with a window facing the side of a Chinese restaurant. At night the ventilation fan shuddered through the wall like something trying to get in.

By day I temped in Midtown offices, answering telephones in other people’s names. At night I wrote at a card table and mailed scripts to theaters whose programs I had never seen. Each submission required a synopsis, a résumé, a self-addressed envelope, and money I did not have at Kinko’s. The rejections returned with impressive reliability. A few contained encouraging notes, which I memorized. “Strong command of atmosphere,” one said, and for weeks I walked around believing atmosphere might be enough.

After eighteen months, my friend Mara agreed to direct *Winter Arithmetic*. We rented a forty-seat theater below a social club in the East Village for four performances. The actors worked for wine and the promise of future employment. I spent my savings on the deposit, insurance, and five hundred postcards, most of which we left in stacks beside café cash registers. My mother called to ask whether the play would be reviewed. I told her it was possible, because possibility was the currency I had left.

Opening night drew eleven people. Six were friends of the cast, two were my roommates, and one man slept from the second scene until the actors turned on a lamp. During the last speech, someone upstairs began dragging furniture across the floor. I sat in the back with my notebook open, pretending to take notes so no one would see my face. Afterward we went to a bar and spoke with the forced tenderness of people visiting a patient whose condition they had agreed not to mention.

To our astonishment, a downtown weekly sent a critic to the second performance. His review appeared the following Thursday. He praised Mara’s “economical staging” and called the play “sincere, atmospheric, and almost entirely inert.” I cut it out and put it in a drawer. I have never understood why we keep the evidence we would never show a jury.

On closing night we struck the set ourselves. There was little to strike: two chairs, a kitchen table, and a doorframe that had cost more than my first month’s rent. Mara and I carried the table to the curb and stood beside it while trucks hissed through the rain. She said, kindly, “Next time, write something you’d pay to see.” I nearly ended our friendship over that sentence. She was right, of course, though it took me years to hear the generosity in it.

I used to describe that period as the time New York tried to beat the ambition out of me. It is a flattering version. The city was not trying anything; it was simply indifferent. What failure took from me, slowly and without ceremony, was the belief that suffering for a play made the play good. Once that was gone, there was less romance in the work and more work in it.

The Monday after closing, I returned to a desk in Midtown. At lunch I wrote a scene about a woman unable to operate the dishwasher in her dead mother’s house. It was plain, almost nothing happened, and for once I knew what every silence was for. The scene was no good either, though not in the old way. I finished it before my lunch hour ended, then went back upstairs and answered the telephone in someone else’s name.

title: memoir|a playwright's early years of failure in New York
text:
I found the box last October while looking for a tax receipt, wedged behind the water heater in my study. It was a cardboard file box, the kind sold in bulk at Staples, and its corners had softened with age. Inside were my twenties. Not photographs, though there were a few, but rejection letters. Hundreds of them. Cream vellum from agents, photocopied form letters from nonprofit theaters, handwritten notes from literary managers who had clearly run out of ways to say no without sounding cruel. I sat on the floor and read them until my knees ached, and for the first time in years, I could smell the radiator steam of that walk-up on West Forty-Sixth Street.

I arrived in New York in September of 1997 with two suitcases and a play about a drowning that I thought would change everything. The city had other plans. I rented a room the size of a taxicab in Hell's Kitchen, five flights up, where the bathtub sat in the kitchen behind a plywood folding door and the window looked directly into a brick wall so close I could touch it without leaning. Mornings began with the screech of the B-D-F line at the Fiftieth Street station, and I would lie there counting the seconds between trains, trying to convince myself that the rhythm sounded like dialogue. It did not. It sounded like a city indifferent to metaphor.

For three years, I worked the light board at an Off-Off-Broadway house on St. Marks Place for seventy-five dollars a week. The theater seated forty-seven people if everyone exhaled, and on most nights, seventeen showed up. I watched my own plays die there, not with the quick mercy of a bad review, but with the slow suffocation of empty seats. During one particularly grim February run of a three-character drama set in a funeral home, the audience consisted of my girlfriend, a man who had wandered in to escape the snow, and a critic from a weekly paper who fell asleep in the second act and left during the blackout. I stood in the booth, my finger hovering over the cue for a thunderclap, and realized I was performing resuscitation on a corpse.

The poverty was not romantic. It was a bone-level exhaustion that manifested in small humiliations. I stole rolls from the diner on Ninth Avenue. I watered down dish soap. I once spent an hour in the drama section of the Strand, reading the first acts of new plays I could not afford to buy, my breath fogging the winter glass of the storefront. At parties in Brooklyn lofts, always arriving late to miss the cover charge, I learned to balance a plastic cup of wine and nod intelligently while inside I was calculating whether I had enough subway fare to get home. The young artists around me seemed to be building cathedrals. I was digging a hole, and I was proud of the symmetry of its walls.

Then came the winter of 2000, though it could have been any winter. A reading at a midtown library branch, one of those fluorescent community rooms where the chairs squeaked and the coffee came from a metal urn. I had rewritten the drowning play fourteen times. Seven people attended. Afterward, an elderly woman in a cloth coat told me it was interesting, which is the word New Yorkers use when they wish they had stayed home. I walked to Times Square in sleet, past the neon and the tourists, and stood under the awning of a shuttered souvenir shop. I was twenty-seven. I had failed publicly, privately, and repeatedly. And standing there, my cheap shoes filling with slush, I felt something unexpected: relief. The worst had happened, and I was still upright. The city had not swallowed me. It had merely tested the elasticity of my want.

I kept writing. Not because I had faith, but because I no longer had anything to lose. The plays that followed were leaner, hungrier, and finally, eventually, produced. But those years in the wilderness were not a prelude to my real life. They were the furnace. Reading those letters now, I do not wince. I remember the walk-ups, the stolen rolls, the empty seats, and I am grateful for the particular education of being unseen. It taught me that a playwright's first loyalty is not to applause, but to the stubborn, private work of bearing witness, even when no one is watching.

title: memoir|a son's search for the father he barely knew
text:
Eleven Minutes

Everything I knew about my father fit on half an index card. Dale Mohn. Born 1961, somewhere near Lima, Ohio. Six feet tall, according to my mother, though the only evidence was a photo from 1986: him at a lake in a gray windbreaker, holding a three-year-old me, his thumb hooked through the loop of my overalls. He smoked Camel Lights. He left in the spring of 1987. He sent forty dollars a week, then forty a month, then a Christmas card, then nothing.

I have one memory, and my mother says I was too young to have kept it, so I probably built it out of the photograph. In it, Dale is changing a porch light with me on his shoulders, singing along to the radio with all the words wrong on purpose. That's it. That's the whole archive.

The year I turned twenty-six—the age he was when he left—I did the math at my own birthday party and had to go stand in the kitchen. That night I Googled him. There were only three Dale Mohns in the country with listed numbers: one in Oregon, one dead in Florida, one in Pahrump, Nevada, sixty miles west of Vegas. A people-search site took my $29.95 and spat out his known associates, including a woman named Darla, 1989 to 1994. I drafted the letter nine times. Dear Dale. Dear Dad. Dear Mr. Mohn.

He called three weeks later, a Tuesday, while I sat in my car outside the school where I teach algebra. We talked for eleven minutes. I had a legal pad full of questions and asked none of them. He asked three: how's your mother, where do you live, you married? He didn't apologize. He said, "Well. You sound all right," like he was signing off on an inspection.

I flew out over spring break. Pahrump is billboards and gravel, a winery in the desert, the town Art Bell used to broadcast from. Dale's trailer was beige, cinder-block porch, a heeler named Motor. I hadn't expected the oxygen tubing. Thirty years of Camels, he said, and shrugged. He'd gone soft and gray; the windbreaker man was in there somewhere. We watched a race with the volume low. He made me a bologna sandwich I didn't ask for, cut corner to corner—which is how I cut mine.

On the TV tray was a shoebox. Inside: his copy of the lake photo, more worn than mine, and a birthday card, undated, addressed to "Buddy" in careful block letters. Never sent. He didn't explain it and I didn't ask. Some things you don't want the actual answer to.

On the drive back over the hump toward the Vegas lights, I noticed my thumbs on the rental wheel. They're his. I'd just never seen his before.

We talk now, once a month, give or take. Eleven minutes. It isn't enough. I'm keeping it anyway.

title: parenting guide|helping teenagers manage screen time
text:
Chapter 5: From Screen Police to Screen Coach

At 10:47 p.m., you notice light beneath your teenager’s bedroom door. You have already asked twice for the phone to be put away. Every instinct says, *Take it. Cancel the data plan. End this tonight.*

Sometimes a firm boundary is necessary. But if screen time has become a nightly contest, confiscation may win the battle without teaching the skill your teenager actually needs: managing technology when you are not there.

I encourage parents to think of themselves less as screen police and more as coaches. A coach does not simply blow the whistle; a coach helps players notice what is happening, practise better habits, and recover after mistakes.

 Start with curiosity, not a courtroom

“Screen time” describes many different activities. Your teenager might be messaging a lonely friend, editing a video, avoiding homework, playing with teammates, or scrolling because sleep feels impossible. The number of hours matters, but it does not tell the whole story.

Before changing the rules, spend a week observing patterns: sleep, mood, schoolwork, movement, family connection, and conflict around devices. Then choose a calm moment—not the middle of an argument—and say something like:

“I’ve noticed mornings have been rough, and I wonder whether late-night scrolling is part of it. I’m not asking to catch you out. How is your phone working for you right now?”

Ask what your teenager enjoys, what feels hard to stop, and what they wish were different. Listen without turning every answer into evidence for your case. Collaboration does not mean giving up parental authority; it means including the person whose cooperation you need.

 Build a short, specific agreement

A useful family plan usually contains a handful of clear anchors rather than an elaborate system of minute-by-minute accounting. You might agree on:

- Sleep: Devices charge outside the bedroom, with a wind-down period before bed.
- Meals: Everyone, including adults, keeps phones off the table.
- Schoolwork: Entertainment apps stay closed during agreed study blocks, with genuine breaks.
- Driving and safety: No handheld phone use, without exception.
- Exceptions: How to handle group projects, travel, ill health, or an important conversation.

Let your teenager help choose the details and suggest what should happen when the agreement slips. Write it down, keep it visible, and set a date to review it. A plan that works for a fourteen-year-old may be too restrictive at seventeen.

 Make the desired behaviour easier
